Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary clinics (HC II/III) in Uganda predominantly use paper-based registers for patient data recording at point of care, including outpatient/inpatient registers, lab forms, and HMIS tools. Aggregate data from these paper forms is later transcribed into DHIS2 at district level for reporting, leading to errors and delays. Digital systems like EMRs (e.g., UgandaEMR) and DHIS2 are available in higher facilities (HCIV+) but mostly program-specific (HIV), with hybrid paper-digital dominant (94%+ HCIVs); pure digital rare (1-2%). Pilots like Stre@mline exist in select rural hospitals but not scaled nationally. Barriers include unreliable electricity/internet in rural areas (~12% stable connectivity), staff shortages, high turnover, poor ICT infrastructure, and donor-driven silos. National policies (2023-2025 Digital Health Strategy) aim for point-of-care digital by 2025/26, but rural reality lags, with paper default and digital for upward reporting only.

revision_notes: Fetched the two reachable cited sources (the MIT DINT article returned a 403 and could not be verified). The 2025 cross-sectional BMC study (265 government facilities) confirms 94.3% use a hybrid of paper and electronic records, with only 1.9% purely digital, supporting a 'some digital' element rather than 'entirely paper'. A June 2025 Ministry of Health account confirms EMR rollout (Clinic Master/eAFYA) has reached only 5 Health Centre IVs and 2 Health Centre IIIs nationally as the main programme, but the disease-specific Uganda EMR (HIV/TB) is deployed at 'selected health centre IIs' as ART sites, meaning some rural primary clinics do capture some patient data digitally at point of care. Recalculated from 1 (Entirely paper) to 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) since the evidence, read in full, shows a minority digital presence at rural facility level rather than none. Not a top-of-scale promotion so no escalation required.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare facilities (Health Centre II/III) in Uganda continue to rely predominantly on paper-based registers, including outpatient, inpatient, maternity and HMIS tools, for point-of-care data capture. Nationally, 94.3% of surveyed public health facilities operate a hybrid of paper and electronic record systems, with purely digital record-keeping present in only 1.9% of facilities. The Ministry of Health's main Electronic Medical Records rollout (Clinic Master and eAFYA) had, by 2025, reached only 5 Health Centre IVs and 2 Health Centre IIIs nationwide, concentrating instead on national, regional and general hospitals. However, the disease-specific UgandaEMR platform for HIV/TB patients is deployed at selected Health Centre II ART sites, so some rural clinics do capture a subset of patient data digitally alongside continued paper-based routine registers. This combination of a dominant paper default with a minority of digital, programme-specific data capture characterises rural clinics as mostly paper with some digital elements.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Rural police stations in Uganda predominantly use paper-based recording for case files, complaints, and incidents. Standard practice involves manual entry in hard-backed occurrence books as the foundation document for all reports, with no evidence of digital replacement at station level, especially rural ones lacking infrastructure (no reliable electricity, internet, or computers). A 2017 Crime Records Management System (CRMS) was developed for CID case tracking, piloted only in 10 Kampala divisions—not rural or station-level. Judiciary is digitizing (ECCMIS), but police stations remain manual per UK DFID 1998 evaluation (still relevant as no rural rollout found). US State Dept HR reports describe investigations without noting digital tools at stations. UNODC notes digital in prosecution/judiciary, not police. Annual crime reports imply aggregate data entry post-paper collection. Score 1: entirely paper-based at rural facilities.

revised_comments: Rural police stations in Uganda continue to record case files, complaints and incidents using paper-based occurrence books and hard files at the point of service. The Crime Records Management System (CRMS), developed from 2013 and first piloted in ten Kampala Metropolitan divisions from 2017, was upgraded in 2021 but as of that upgrade remained under testing beyond Kampala, with no confirmed extension to rural stations. The 2025 Sub-County Policing Model focuses on deploying personnel to every sub-county, and a new Crime Data Analysis Centre opened in 2025 as a centralised analytics hub at Police Headquarters, but neither initiative digitises data capture at individual rural police stations. Record-keeping at rural stations therefore remains entirely paper-based.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices (86% of 152 total birth/death registration offices at district level) conduct birth registration using paper-based processes at the point of service. Data is later entered digitally at regional levels and transferred via CDs/flash drives to national database. All local offices have computers, but registration remains manual/paper. Mobile Vital Record System (piloted 2013 with UNICEF) enables birth notifications from rural areas via mobile to central database, but full registration still requires paper at district registries. Low completeness (~32% children under 5 registered, 2016). Barriers: distance (>10km to offices, up to 4hr travel), low awareness, costs for certificates. National digital ID push (2025-26 MOSIP migration 28M+ records) focuses on IDs, not CRVS point-of-service in rural registries. Pilots like mobile notification indicate some digital elements, but default is paper at rural facilities. Gap: National ambitions for integrated digital ID/CRVS exist, but rural point-of-registration lags due to infrastructure/connectivity issues. (178 words)

revision_notes: Fetched the Uganda Vital Statistics Report 2024 (UBOS, published July 2025); the original 2019 CRVS snapshot is now dated but broadly consistent. Fresh searches confirm the Mobile Vital Records System (MVRS, operating since 2014) still requires paper-based notification and registration forms at Sub-County/Division offices, with district-level staff entering details into the digital MVRS database (135 hospitals and 117 district registration centres). A 2025 study using 2020-2024 NIRA administrative data (2.3m+ birth notifications) confirms persistent rural-urban gaps in registration timeliness, consistent with paper-driven, facility-dependent processes in rural areas. A 2025 URSB-NIRA handover speech confirms marriage records have been digitised nationally, but this does not describe rural civil registry offices specifically. Confirmed at 2 (Mostly paper - some digital); evidence continues to support both a paper-dominant registration process and genuine digital elements (computerised entry, digital notification channels).
revised_comments: Rural civil registry offices in Uganda register births and other vital events primarily through paper-based forms completed at Sub-County or Division offices at the point of service. The Mobile Vital Records System (MVRS), operational since 2014 through a partnership between the Uganda Registration Services Bureau, UNICEF and a telecom operator, supports digital birth notification and processing across 135 hospitals and 117 district-level registration centres, with district staff entering notification details into the digital MVRS database rather than registration occurring digitally at first point of contact. Administrative data covering 2020-2024 shows persistent rural-urban disparities in registration timeliness, consistent with a facility- and paper-dependent registration process in rural areas. Marriage records have been digitised nationally through the National Marriage Registration System, though this affects national administration more than rural point-of-service registration. Overall, rural registry offices combine a dominant paper-based registration process with partial digital elements such as computerised data entry and digital notification channels.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Uganda predominantly use paper-based registers for recording administrative data, attendance, and learning outcomes at the point of service. Head teachers fill extensive paper forms for the Annual School Census (ASC), which are submitted to District Education Offices (DEOs) and manually entered into national EMIS systems.UNESCO EMIS Uganda Case Study%20and%20Data%20for%20Increased%20Resilience%20to%20Crisis_%20country%20case%20study_%20Uganda.pdf) EMIS data collection stalled post-2017 due to poor coverage and quality from paper processes. Digital pilots exist, such as DHIS2-DEMIS (termly paper tools digitized at district level in 10/175 sites since 2019, including rural Gulu/Entebbe) and SMS attendance (eduTrac in 37 districts, SESIL in rural West Nile).DHIS2 Uganda No evidence of majority rural schools using digital tools routinely at point-of-service; daily attendance remains manual, aggregated on paper. Key barriers: lack of electricity (13% rural households connected), computers/internet, trained staff, poor roads limiting verification; rural-urban digital divide stark.Afrobarometer National EMIS ambitions contrast with rural paper reality, reliant on donor pilots not scaled nationwide.

revision_notes: Fetched the DHIS2 case study and the Afrobarometer dispatch; the Education Cannot Wait PDF link in the original citation was malformed/broken and could not be fetched. Fresh searches confirm rural primary schools still submit paper Annual School Census forms for manual EMIS entry, while DHIS2-DEMIS remains a limited pilot (a July 2025 GPE blog describes it scaling from district to school level in Gulu district as part of an ongoing KIX-SEEDS research project, still not nationwide). The TELA biometric/GPS teacher-attendance tool was piloted in around 920 schools across ten Eastern Uganda districts from 2019 but stalled due to a funding shortfall, per a 2024 government report, and has not been confirmed as scaled since. The 2025 Baseline Education Census gathers infrastructure/enrolment data for all 88,242 schools nationally but is a periodic census exercise, not routine digital data capture at school level. Confirmed at 2 (Mostly paper - some digital); no evidence supports either 1 (entirely paper, given confirmed digital pilots) or 3+ (given pilots remain small-scale and unscaled).
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Uganda continue to rely predominantly on paper-based registers for recording attendance and administrative data at the point of service, with head teachers completing manual Annual School Census forms that are later entered into the national Education Management Information System. Digital pilots operate in a minority of rural schools: the DHIS2-DEMIS platform supports termly data capture in a small number of districts, including Gulu in Northern Uganda, where a 2025 initiative is extending it from district to school level, and the TELA biometric and GPS-based attendance tool was piloted in around 920 schools across ten Eastern Uganda districts from 2019 but has not been scaled nationally, in part due to funding constraints and limited rural electricity and internet coverage. A 2025 national Baseline Education Census recorded basic infrastructure and enrolment data across all schools, but this is a periodic census exercise rather than routine digital data capture at school level. Paper remains the default for day-to-day record-keeping in rural primary schools, with digital tools present only in specific pilot districts.
